The [Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") defeated the [Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") in the first [AFL–NFL World Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_World_Championship_Game "AFL–NFL World Championship Game") ([Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")).

The [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") is the annual [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") game that determines the champion of the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL). The game culminates a [season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_regular_season "National Football League regular season") that begins in the previous calendar year, and is the conclusion of the [NFL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_playoffs "National Football League playoffs"). The winner receives the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy"). The contest is held in an American city, chosen three to four years beforehand,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-1) usually at warm-weather sites or [domed stadiums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium#Types "Stadium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-2) Since January 1971, the winner of the [American Football Conference (AFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Championship_Game "AFC Championship Game") has faced the winner of the [National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_Championship_Game "NFC Championship Game") in the culmination of the NFL playoffs.

Before the [1970 merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_merger "AFL–NFL merger") between the [American Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League "American Football League") (AFL) and the NFL, the two leagues met in four such contests. The first two were marketed as the "AFL–NFL World Championship Game", but were also casually referred to as "the Super Bowl game" during the television broadcast.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-3)[Super Bowl III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_III "Super Bowl III") in January 1969 was the first such game that carried the "Super Bowl" moniker in official marketing; the names "[Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")" and "[Super Bowl II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II")" were retroactively applied to the first two games.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-nflaflwcg-4)

A total of 20 franchises, including teams that have relocated to another city or changed their name, have won the Super Bowl.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-record-5) There are four [NFL teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_team "NFL team") that have never appeared in a Super Bowl: the [Cleveland Browns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns"), [Detroit Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Lions "Detroit Lions"), [Jacksonville Jaguars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Jaguars "Jacksonville Jaguars"), and [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans"), though both the Browns ([1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_NFL_Championship_Game "1950 NFL Championship Game"), [1954](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_NFL_Championship_Game "1954 NFL Championship Game"), [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_NFL_Championship_Game "1955 NFL Championship Game"), [1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_NFL_Championship_Game "1964 NFL Championship Game")) and Lions ([1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_NFL_Championship_Game "1935 NFL Championship Game"), [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_NFL_Championship_Game "1952 NFL Championship Game"), [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_NFL_Championship_Game "1953 NFL Championship Game"), [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_NFL_Championship_Game "1957 NFL Championship Game")) had won [NFL Championship Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Championship_Game "NFL Championship Game") prior to the creation of the Super Bowl in the [1966 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NFL_season "1966 NFL season").

The [1972 Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Miami_Dolphins_season "1972 Miami Dolphins season") capped off the only [perfect season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_season "Perfect season") in [NFL history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_National_Football_League "History of the National Football League") with their victory in [Super Bowl VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"). Only two franchises have ever won the Super Bowl while hosting at their home stadiums: the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") in [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") and the [Los Angeles Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl LVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVI "Super Bowl LVI"). The reigning champions are the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") following their victory over the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") in [Super Bowl LX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX "Super Bowl LX").

## Streaks and rematches

### Consecutive wins

[![Image 37](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/1986_Jeno%27s_Pizza_-_46_-_Terry_Bradshaw_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1986_Jeno's_Pizza_-_46_-_Terry_Bradshaw_(cropped).jpg)

The [Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") defeated the [Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV") to win an unprecedented four championships in six years.

Eight franchises have won consecutive Super Bowls, one of which (Pittsburgh) has accomplished it twice:

*   [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") (Super Bowls [I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I") and [II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II"))
*   [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Dolphins "Miami Dolphins") ([VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII") and [VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VIII "Super Bowl VIII"))
*   [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") (twice: [IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IX "Super Bowl IX") and [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_X "Super Bowl X"); [XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIII "Super Bowl XIII") and [XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV"))
*   [San Francisco 49ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_49ers "San Francisco 49ers") ([XXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIII "Super Bowl XXIII") and [XXIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIV "Super Bowl XXIV"))
*   [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") ([XXVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVII "Super Bowl XXVII") and [XXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVIII "Super Bowl XXVIII"))
*   [Denver Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Broncos "Denver Broncos") ([XXXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXII "Super Bowl XXXII") and [XXXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXIII "Super Bowl XXXIII"))[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-BroncosStreaks-94)
*   [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") ([XXXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXVIII "Super Bowl XXXVIII") and [XXXIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXIX "Super Bowl XXXIX"))
*   [Kansas City Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") ([LVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII "Super Bowl LVII") and [LVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVIII "Super Bowl LVIII"))

Although no franchise to date has won three Super Bowls in a row, several have had eras of sustained success, nearly accomplishing a [three-peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-peat "Three-peat"):

*   The [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") won the first two Super Bowls, and also won the [NFL Championship Game the preceding year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_NFL_Championship_Game "1965 NFL Championship Game"). If the Super Bowl had been instituted that year, the Packers would have qualified and faced the Buffalo Bills of the AFL.
*   The [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Dolphins "Miami Dolphins") appeared in three consecutive Super Bowls ([VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VI "Super Bowl VI"), [VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"), and [VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VIII "Super Bowl VIII"))– winning the last two.
*   The [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") won two consecutive Super Bowls ([IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IX "Super Bowl IX") and [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_X "Super Bowl X")); they also won two more consecutive Super Bowls ([XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIII "Super Bowl XIII") and [XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XIV "Super Bowl XIV")) for four titles in six seasons.
*   The [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") won two consecutive Super Bowls ([XXVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVII "Super Bowl XXVII") and [XXVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXVIII "Super Bowl XXVIII")); the [Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Dallas_Cowboys_season "1995 Dallas Cowboys season") won [Super Bowl XXX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXX "Super Bowl XXX") the following year for three titles in four seasons.
*   The [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") won Super Bowls [XLIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLIX "Super Bowl XLIX"), [LI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LI "Super Bowl LI"), and [LIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIII "Super Bowl LIII") for three titles in five seasons. They also appeared in and lost [Super Bowl LII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LII "Super Bowl LII") to the [Philadelphia Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Philadelphia_Eagles_season "2017 Philadelphia Eagles season") following the 2017 season, giving them four Super Bowl appearances in five years.
*   The [Kansas City Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") came the closest to a three-peat, winning back-to-back Super Bowls in [LVII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII "Super Bowl LVII") and [LVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVIII "Super Bowl LVIII") but losing their third consecutive appearance in [LIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIX "Super Bowl LIX"). They additionally won [LIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LIV "Super Bowl LIV") several years beforehand, and lost [LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV"), for a total of five Super Bowl appearances in six seasons.

The [Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") defeated the [Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Chiefs "Kansas City Chiefs") in the first [AFL–NFL World Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_World_Championship_Game "AFL–NFL World Championship Game") ([Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")).

The [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") is the annual [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") game that determines the champion of the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL). The game culminates a [season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_regular_season "National Football League regular season") that begins in the previous calendar year, and is the conclusion of the [NFL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_playoffs "National Football League playoffs"). The winner receives the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy"). The contest is held in an American city, chosen three to four years beforehand,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-1) usually at warm-weather sites or [domed stadiums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium#Types "Stadium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-2) Since January 1971, the winner of the [American Football Conference (AFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Championship_Game "AFC Championship Game") has faced the winner of the [National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFC_Championship_Game "NFC Championship Game") in the culmination of the NFL playoffs.

Before the [1970 merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93NFL_merger "AFL–NFL merger") between the [American Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League "American Football League") (AFL) and the NFL, the two leagues met in four such contests. The first two were marketed as the "AFL–NFL World Championship Game", but were also casually referred to as "the Super Bowl game" during the television broadcast.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-3)[Super Bowl III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_III "Super Bowl III") in January 1969 was the first such game that carried the "Super Bowl" moniker in official marketing; the names "[Super Bowl I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_I "Super Bowl I")" and "[Super Bowl II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_II "Super Bowl II")" were retroactively applied to the first two games.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-nflaflwcg-4)

A total of 20 franchises, including teams that have relocated to another city or changed their name, have won the Super Bowl.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Super_Bowl_champions#cite_note-record-5) There are four [NFL teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_team "NFL team") that have never appeared in a Super Bowl: the [Cleveland Browns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns"), [Detroit Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Lions "Detroit Lions"), [Jacksonville Jaguars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Jaguars "Jacksonville Jaguars"), and [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans"), though both the Browns ([1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_NFL_Championship_Game "1950 NFL Championship Game"), [1954](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_NFL_Championship_Game "1954 NFL Championship Game"), [1955](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_NFL_Championship_Game "1955 NFL Championship Game"), [1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_NFL_Championship_Game "1964 NFL Championship Game")) and Lions ([1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_NFL_Championship_Game "1935 NFL Championship Game"), [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_NFL_Championship_Game "1952 NFL Championship Game"), [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_NFL_Championship_Game "1953 NFL Championship Game"), [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_NFL_Championship_Game "1957 NFL Championship Game")) had won [NFL Championship Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Championship_Game "NFL Championship Game") prior to the creation of the Super Bowl in the [1966 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NFL_season "1966 NFL season").

The [1972 Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Miami_Dolphins_season "1972 Miami Dolphins season") capped off the only [perfect season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_season "Perfect season") in [NFL history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_National_Football_League "History of the National Football League") with their victory in [Super Bowl VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_VII "Super Bowl VII"). Only two franchises have ever won the Super Bowl while hosting at their home stadiums: the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") in [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") and the [Los Angeles Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") in [Super Bowl LVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVI "Super Bowl LVI"). The reigning champions are the [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks "Seattle Seahawks") following their victory over the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") in [Super Bowl LX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX "Super Bowl LX").

The 2022 NFL draft was the National Football League's 87th annual draft and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the Caesars Forum on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise next to Las Vegas. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the Las Vegas metropolitan area and the state of Nevada.

The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in 1991. Along with the 1972 and 2000 drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five Georgia defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since 2013. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since 1997, and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since 2014.

A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.[1]

Host cityedit

Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the 2020 NFL draft, coinciding with the Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic the draft was held as a virtual event. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.[2]

Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating red carpet on the man-made lake in front of the Bellagio and its fountains. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.[3][4]

Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event.[3][4] The Linq Promenade hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities.[3][4] Parts of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.[5]

Resolution JC-2A selectionsedit

Resolution JC-2A, enacted by the NFL in November 2020, rewards teams for developing minority candidates for head coach and/or general manager positions.[16] The resolution rewards teams whose minority candidates are hired away for one of those positions by awarding draft selections, which are at the end of the third round, after standard compensatory selections; if multiple teams qualify, they are awarded by draft order in the first round. These picks are in addition to, and have no impact on, the standard 32 compensatory selections.[17] Seven picks were awarded for the 2022 draft pursuant to the resolution.

 Cleveland received a third-round selection (99th overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Minnesota hiring vice president of football operations Kwesi Adofo-Mensah as general manager.[6]
 Baltimore received a third-round selection (100th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Houston hiring assistant head coach and passing game coordinator David Culley as head coach.[7]
 New Orleans received a third-round selection (101st overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Atlanta hiring pro scouting director Terry Fontenot as general manager.[8]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (102nd overall), a 2021 third-round selection and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for the NY Jets hiring defensive coordinator Robert Saleh as head coach and Washington hiring vice president of player personnel Martin Mayhew as general manager.[9][10][11]
 Kansas City received a third-round selection (103rd overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Chicago hiring executive director of player personnel Ryan Poles as general manager.[12]
 The LA Rams received a third-round selection (104th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Detroit hiring college scouting director Brad Holmes as general manager.[13]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (105th overall) and another 2023 third-round selection when Miami hired offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as head coach.[14]
Notesedit
 Players are identified as Pro Bowlers if they were selected for the Pro Bowl at any time in their career.

Forfeited selections

 New Orleans forfeited a sixth-round selection as a penalty for repeated violations of the league's COVID-19 guidelines.[15]

The 2022 NFL draft was the National Football League's 87th annual draft and was held from April 28–30, 2022, at the Caesars Forum on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise next to Las Vegas. The first round was held on Thursday, April 28, and was followed by the second and third rounds on Friday, April 29. The draft concluded with rounds 4–7 on Saturday, April 30. It was the first draft to be held in the Las Vegas metropolitan area and the state of Nevada.

The first five selections were defensive players, the second-most taken at the start of a draft after the six in 1991. Along with the 1972 and 2000 drafts, it marked the third time defensive players were the first two picks after the first three picks in the previous year's draft were quarterbacks. Five Georgia defensive players were taken during the first round, the most from an individual school in a draft. In addition to the high number of defensive selections, nine offensive linemen were taken in the first round, the most since 2013. Conversely, only one quarterback was selected in the first round at 20th overall, the lowest for a draft's first quarterback since 1997, and no running backs were taken in the first round for the first time since 2014.

A record nine draft-day trades with first-round picks were made, which resulted in less than half of the first-round selections being made by the teams that initially owned them. Analysts attributed the high number of trades to eight teams entering the draft without a first-round selection and a general absence of highly touted prospects.[1]

Host cityedit

Las Vegas was originally scheduled to host the 2020 NFL draft, coinciding with the Oakland Raiders' relocation to the city. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic the draft was held as a virtual event. Las Vegas was given the 2022 Draft as a result.[2]

Draft activities were held around two main locations on the Las Vegas Strip; invited players walked a floating red carpet on the man-made lake in front of the Bellagio and its fountains. The plans were similar to those originally intended for the 2020 draft, although a plan for players to be transported onto the stage by boat was scrapped in favor of using walkways.[3][4]

Caesars Forum housed infrastructure for the event.[3][4] The Linq Promenade hosted the NFL Draft Experience, which featured fan activities.[3][4] Parts of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard were closed to vehicle traffic to allow spectators to travel between the two sites.[5]

(PD) indicates trades completed prior to the start of the draft (i.e. Pre-Draft), while (D) denotes trades which took place during the 2022 draft.

Round 1

 No. 7: Chicago → NY Giants (PD). Chicago traded first- and fourth-round selections (7th and 112th overall), and 2021 first- and fourth-round selections to the NY Giants in exchange for a 2021 first-round selection.[trade 1]
 No. 9: Denver → Seattle (PD). Denver traded first-, second- and fifth-round selections (9th, 40th and 145th overall), 2023 first- and second-round selections, QB Drew Lock, TE Noah Fant and DT Shelby Harris to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a fourth-round selection (116th overall) and QB Russell Wilson.[trade 2]
 No. 10: Seattle → NY Jets (PD). Seattle traded a first-round selection (10th overall), 2021 first- and third-round selections, and S Bradley McDougald to the NY Jets in exchange for a fourth-round selection (109th overall) and S Jamal Adams.[trade 3]
 No. 11: Washington → New Orleans (D). Washington traded a first-round selection (11th overall) to New Orleans in exchange for first-, third- and fourth-round selections (16th, 98th and 120th overall).[trade 4]
 No. 12: Minnesota → Detroit (D). Minnesota traded first- and second-round selections (12th and 46th overall) to the Detroit Lions in exchange for first-, second- and third-round selections (32nd, 34th and 66th overall).[trade 4]
 No. 13: Cleveland → Houston → Philadelphia. Multiple trades:
       Cleveland → Houston (PD). Cleveland traded first- and fourth-round selections (13th and 107th overall), 2023 first- and third-round selections, and 2024 first- and fourth-round selections to Houston in exchange for a 2024 sixth-round selection and QB Deshaun Watson.[trade 5]

 No. 15: Miami → Philadelphia → Houston. Multiple trades:
       Miami → Philadelphia (PD). Miami traded a first-round selection (15th overall), and 2021 first- and fourth-round selections to Philadelphia in exchange for 2021 first- and fifth-round selections.[trade 6]
       Philadelphia → Houston (D). See Round 1: Houston → Philadelphia.[trade 4]
 No. 16: Indianapolis → Philadelphia → New Orleans → Washington. Multiple trades:
       Indianapolis → Philadelphia (PD). Indianapolis traded a conditional first-round selection (16th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection to Philadelphia in exchange for QB Carson Wentz. The conditional selection was upgraded from the second round because Wentz played 75% of Indianapolis' offensive snaps.[trade 7]
       Philadelphia → New Orleans (PD). Philadelphia traded two first-round selections and a sixth-round selection (16th, 19th and 194th overall) to New Orleans in exchange for first-, third- and seventh-round selections (18th, 101st and 237th overall), a 2023 first-round selection and a 2024 second-round selection.[trade 8]

Resolution JC-2A selectionsedit

Resolution JC-2A, enacted by the NFL in November 2020, rewards teams for developing minority candidates for head coach and/or general manager positions.[16] The resolution rewards teams whose minority candidates are hired away for one of those positions by awarding draft selections, which are at the end of the third round, after standard compensatory selections; if multiple teams qualify, they are awarded by draft order in the first round. These picks are in addition to, and have no impact on, the standard 32 compensatory selections.[17] Seven picks were awarded for the 2022 draft pursuant to the resolution.

 Cleveland received a third-round selection (99th overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Minnesota hiring vice president of football operations Kwesi Adofo-Mensah as general manager.[6]
 Baltimore received a third-round selection (100th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Houston hiring assistant head coach and passing game coordinator David Culley as head coach.[7]
 New Orleans received a third-round selection (101st overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Atlanta hiring pro scouting director Terry Fontenot as general manager.[8]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (102nd overall), a 2021 third-round selection and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for the NY Jets hiring defensive coordinator Robert Saleh as head coach and Washington hiring vice president of player personnel Martin Mayhew as general manager.[9][10][11]
 Kansas City received a third-round selection (103rd overall) and a 2023 third-round selection as compensation for Chicago hiring executive director of player personnel Ryan Poles as general manager.[12]
 The LA Rams received a third-round selection (104th overall) and a 2021 third-round selection as compensation for Detroit hiring college scouting director Brad Holmes as general manager.[13]
 San Francisco received a third-round selection (105th overall) and another 2023 third-round selection when Miami hired offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as head coach.[14]
Notesedit
 Players are identified as Pro Bowlers if they were selected for the Pro Bowl at any time in their career.

Forfeited selections

 New Orleans forfeited a sixth-round selection as a penalty for repeated violations of the league's COVID-19 guidelines.[15]
